senses.definition: A quiet inner prompting of conscience or of God, heard more clearly in calm and attention than in noise or pressure.

core.definition: A quiet inner prompting of conscience or of God, heard more clearly in calm and attention than in noise or pressure.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on VOICE, with weaker stress on still and small. The small and still both end in a clear dark l, and many learners put too much force on the vowel in voice.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests gentle, trustworthy guidance that comes in quiet moments.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase mostly in religious talk, writing, or reflective conversation about conscience or intuition. It is not a sound you literally hear in everyday life, and using it casually can sound a bit sentimental. A natural reply is 'Yeah, I think that was the right call,' sometimes with a nod to faith.

distinctions.note: A gut feeling is an everyday, informal sense of intuition; a still small voice suggests a more reflective or spiritual prompting.
Conscience is the general moral sense; the still small voice is a more poetic image of that sense being heard in stillness.
Inner voice is a broader, more neutral term that does not necessarily carry religious associations.

collocations: the still small voice of conscience
the still small voice of God
listen for the still small voice

examples.everyday: I wanted to argue, but a still small voice told me to just let it go.
examples.professional: The team lead didn't push back on the data, but a still small voice kept asking whether we had checked the labels.
examples.analytical: Christian writers have long read Elijah's encounter at Horeb as teaching that God often speaks through quiet attentiveness rather than spectacle.

nuance.analogy: Like a faint radio station you can only hear once the noisy room goes quiet.
nuance.etymology: From 1 Kings 19:12 in the King James Version; 'still' comes from Old English stille, meaning quiet.
common_mistakes: Using the phrase for a literal whisper in ordinary speech, where it sounds overly poetic.
Pronouncing still to rhyme with steel instead of fill.
nuance.biblical_note: In 1 Kings 19:11-13, the prophet Elijah stands on Mount Horeb and experiences a great wind, an earthquake and a fire, but the Lord is not in them. After the fire comes what the Revised Standard Version renders as a sound of sheer silence, and Elijah covers his face and goes out to meet God. The Hebrew phrase is qol demamah daqqah, a voice of thin silence or gentle whisper. The phrase still small voice comes from the King James Version, not the RSV, so the RSV reader should look for the sound of silence in 1 Kings 19:12. Related passages are 1 Kings 19:9-10 and 1 Kings 19:13.

senses.definition: In AI: A small set of extra trainable layers added to a frozen model so it can be fine-tuned cheaply.
Specifically, a device that permits two or more plugs to be used at a single electrical power point.
senses.example: The wall outlet sprouted an electrical monstrosity of adapters plugged into adapters that sparked ominously.

senses.definition: Specifically, a device that allows one format of plug to be used with a different format of socket.
senses.example: We bought adapters to use our three-prong plugs in the two-prong, unpolarized outlets of the old house.

senses.definition: Specifically, an AC adapter: a device that reduces voltage and converts AC to DC to allow a battery-powered device to use mains power.
senses.example: I lost my cellphone's adapter so I couldn't recharge it.

senses.definition: A collection of low-rank matrices which, when added to a base model, produces a fine-tuned model; a LoRA.
One who is capable of adapting to differing situations.
senses.example: He was an able adapter, and could easily adjust to the differences when the company changed ownership.

senses.definition: One who adapts a thing, e.g. a play.
senses.example: The critic gave rave reviews to the adapter of the ancient play, who worked to give the text more relevance to the modern day.

senses.definition: A device or application used to achieve operative compatibility between devices that otherwise are incompatible.
senses.example: He had an adapter that let him plug his phone into the car's cigarette lighter for power.

core.definition: A device that lets a plug from one country or type fit a different power outlet or connector.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable of the root, 'dap.' The final -er is a rhotic American r, so do not say 'uh-DAP-tah.' The t is a flap, so it sounds almost like a d.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical, everyday word.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say adapter for a device that changes one type of plug or connector to another, especially when traveling abroad. In technical settings, adapter also refers to software or AI components. In a store, ask for a 'travel adapter' or 'power adapter' to be clear.

distinctions.note: A converter changes the voltage as well as the plug shape. An adapter only changes the plug shape and does not change voltage.
A charger supplies power to a device. An adapter only connects a plug to a socket and does not provide power by itself.

examples.everyday: Do you have an adapter I can borrow? My phone charger doesn't fit this outlet.
examples.professional: We need a USB-C to HDMI adapter for the conference room projector before the meeting starts.
examples.analytical: In machine learning, an adapter is a small trainable module inserted into a frozen model so the model can be fine-tuned efficiently.

nuance.analogy: Think of an adapter as a translator for plugs. It lets two different shapes understand each other.
nuance.etymology: Formed from adapt, with the agent suffix -er meaning 'one that does something.'
common_mistakes: Using 'adapter' to mean a voltage converter, which is a different device that changes electrical power.
Pronouncing the final -er as 'uh,' which is fine in fast speech, but in careful speech it is pronounced with a clear American r.

conversation.text: An adapter is a small trainable module inserted into a frozen network to handle a new task.
We serve one base model and load a different adapter for each customer.
We wrote an adapter so the new vector store fits our old retrieval interface.
Don't forget a power adapter; the outlets there are different.

senses.definition: Containing, composed of, or consisting of fat; fatty.
Slightly overweight; chubby.
Animal fat stored in the tissue of the body.

core.definition: Made of or containing fat; relating to the body's fat tissue.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the middle vowel is a weak uh, not a clear ih. The final s is a plain s sound, not a z.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in medical and scientific use, but it can sound unkind if used to describe a person.
nuance.usage_note: Doctors, nutritionists and biologists use adipose tissue for body fat, which is the standard term in anatomy. Americans rarely use adipose about people, because it sounds clinical and can be rude. For a person, say overweight or heavyset instead.

distinctions.note: Fatty is everyday and often refers to food; adipose is clinical and refers to body fat tissue.
Obese is a medical term for a serious condition of excess weight; adipose describes the fat tissue itself, not a condition.

examples.everyday: The vet said my cat is carrying too much adipose tissue, so no more treats for a while.
examples.professional: The nutrition study measured visceral adipose tissue in each participant using MRI scans.
examples.analytical: Whether adipose tissue is merely a storage site or an active endocrine organ has reshaped how physiologists understand metabolism.

nuance.analogy: Adipose tissue works like a body's savings account, holding energy in reserve until it is withdrawn.
nuance.etymology: From Latin adeps, adipis, meaning soft fat or lard.
common_mistakes: Using adipose as a friendly word for chubby, which sounds clinical or rude.
Stressing the final syllable as uh-DIPE-ohs; the stress is on the first syllable.

adipose.etymology: From international scientific vocabulary, from New Latin *adipōsus*, from Latin *adeps* (“fat, lard”).

senses.definition: The act of adjudicating, of reaching a judgment.
A judgment or sentence.
The decision upon the question of whether the debtor is a bankrupt.
The process of identifying the type of material or device that set off an alarm and assessing the potential threat with corresponding implications for the need to take further action.

core.definition: The formal process of deciding a dispute or claim, or the official decision itself, made by a judge or panel.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on KAY, the fourth syllable, and the -tion ending is pronounced shun. Keep the other syllables short and unstressed, and do not give each vowel its full value.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it sounds official and somewhat heavy in everyday speech.
nuance.usage_note: Adjudication is used in legal, insurance, sports and academic contexts, such as the adjudication of a claim. In everyday talk Americans say decision, ruling or resolution. The word sounds official and can feel overly formal in casual conversation.

distinctions.note: Decision is everyday and general; adjudication is a formal decision reached through a dispute process.
Arbitration is a private hearing chosen by the parties; adjudication is usually handled by a court or official body.

examples.everyday: The insurance company promised a fast adjudication of my claim, but it took three months.
examples.professional: The data team built an automated adjudication process for flagged records before they reach the warehouse.
examples.analytical: Adjudication presupposes shared standards, which is precisely what is missing in many moral disputes.

nuance.analogy: Adjudication is the final whistle in a formal dispute: it ends the argument with an official call.
nuance.etymology: From Latin adjudicatio, a judging, from adjudicare, to award or judge.
common_mistakes: Using adjudication for general opinions or discussion; it refers to a formal decision.
Stressing the early syllables, as AD-juh-dih-KAY-shun; the main stress is on KAY near the end.

senses.definition: The profession of an advocate.
The act of arguing in favor of, or supporting someone or something.
The practice of supporting someone to make their voice heard.

core.definition: The act of publicly supporting a cause, policy, or person, especially to help others be heard or treated fairly.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on the first syllable, AD. The middle syllables are reduced to a quick schwa sound, and the final syllable is a light 'see.' Do not stress the second syllable as in the verb advocate's final-syllable pattern.

nuance.connotation: Positive in most contexts, since it suggests fighting for a good cause. It can sound negative to someone who opposes the cause being promoted.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use advocacy constantly in health, education, nonprofit, and civil rights contexts, as in patient advocacy or consumer advocacy. It is common in news and professional writing but sounds slightly formal in casual talk, where people often say 'standing up for' or 'pushing for.' A natural follow-up is 'I'm an advocate for' someone or something.

distinctions.note: Lobbying is organized effort to influence lawmakers or government officials, often paid. Advocacy is broader and includes public campaigns, education, and support for people.
Support is a general word for helping or agreeing with someone. Advocacy implies active, public work to promote a cause.

examples.everyday: My mom does a lot of advocacy for seniors at the community center.
examples.professional: Our team's advocacy work helped the company adopt more flexible parental leave.
examples.analytical: Her moral argument functions as advocacy rather than neutral analysis, since she openly seeks to change the reader's view.

nuance.analogy: Like a lawyer who speaks for a client who cannot easily speak for themselves.
nuance.etymology: From Latin advocatus, 'one called to aid,' from advocare, 'to call to.'
common_mistakes: Using advocacy as a verb; the verb is advocate.
Confusing advocacy with lobbying when the activity is not paid or directed at lawmakers.

advocacy.etymology: From Middle English *advocacie*, *advocacye*, *advocatye*, from Middle French *advocacie*, *advocatie*, *avocacie* and Medieval Latin *advocātia*; equivalent to *advocate* + *-cy*.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to an eon.
Eon-long, everlasting.

core.definition: Lasting for an age or eon, or eternal in a theological sense, depending on how the Greek word aiōnios is translated.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, OH, and the first vowel is 'ee.' The final two syllables are reduced to 'nee-un.' Learners often stress the first syllable or pronounce it like 'ay-ON-ee-an.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive in religious or poetic contexts. In theology it can be a contested term, so the connotation depends on the debate.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use aeonian mostly in theology, classics, and literary writing, especially in discussions of biblical Greek. Ordinary speakers would say everlasting or eternal. Note that eonian is also common in American texts, so both spellings are acceptable.

distinctions.note: Eternal means without beginning or end. Aeonian can mean lasting for an age, which may not be endless, depending on the context.
Everlasting is the common English word for something that never ends. Aeonian is more technical and is used mainly in theological discussion of Greek terms.

examples.everyday: Some of those mountains look aeonian, but they are only a few million years old.
examples.professional: The report describes the glacier's ice as if it were aeonian, which overstates its age.
examples.analytical: The debate over Matthew 25:46 hinges on whether aiōnios means eternal or simply aeonian, that is, belonging to an age.

nuance.analogy: Like a timer set to a whole age, not to forever.
nuance.etymology: From Greek aiōn, meaning age, lifetime, or eon.
common_mistakes: Confusing aeonian with eonian; both are used, but learners should be consistent.
Assuming it always means eternal; it can mean lasting for an age.

senses.definition: The king of Persia in the Book of Esther, usually identified with the historical ruler Xerxes I.

core.definition: The king of Persia in the Book of Esther, usually identified with the historical ruler Xerxes I.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the third-from-last syllable, EER. The middle 'su' is pronounced 'shoo' or 'syoo,' and the final syllables are reduced to 'us.'

nuance.connotation: neutral: he is a powerful but easily manipulated ruler in the Esther story.
nuance.usage_note: Americans meet this name in Bible study, especially during the Jewish holiday of Purim, which is connected to the Book of Esther. The name is not used in everyday speech and refers only to the Persian king in the story. Many historians identify him with Xerxes I, the king known from Greek sources.

distinctions.note: Xerxes is the Greek name of the historical king, while Ahasuerus is the Hebrew name used in the Book of Esther.
Artaxerxes is a different Persian king named in Ezra and Nehemiah, not the king of the Esther story.

examples.everyday: At the Purim party, the kids dressed up as characters from the story, and someone asked who King Ahasuerus was.
examples.professional: In the history session, I explained that the name Ahasuerus in Esther is usually linked to Xerxes I of Persia.
examples.analytical: The narrative presents Ahasuerus as a powerful but easily swayed monarch, whose decisions turn on the advice of his courtiers.

nuance.analogy: Ahasuerus is like a famous ruler who appears in a story mainly through the decisions of the people around him.
nuance.etymology: From the Hebrew Ahashverosh, derived from the Old Persian Khshayarsha; the Persian name's exact meaning is disputed.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, saying 'uh-HASS-yoo-ER-us' with the wrong vowel pattern.
Assuming Ahasuerus is a different king from Xerxes without checking the historical identification.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew name Ahashverosh (אֲחַשְׁוֵרוֹשׁ) appears in Esther 1:1 (RSV), which introduces him as the king who reigned from India to Ethiopia over many provinces. Esther 2:16-17 (RSV) describes how he chooses Esther as queen after Vashti is removed. Esther 8:1-2 (RSV) shows him giving Esther and Mordecai authority over Haman's property and the Jewish cause, showing his role as the one who ultimately permits the reversal of the decree.

senses.definition: The conditional part of a hypothetical proposition, i.e. p→q, where p is the antecedent, and q is the consequent.
The first of two subsets of a sequent, consisting of all the sequent's formulae which are valuated as true.
senses.example: (Can we add an example for this sense?)

senses.definition: Any thing that precedes another thing, especially the cause of the second thing.
An ancestor.
A word, phrase or clause referred to by a pronoun or other pro-form.
The first term of a ratio, i.e. the term a in the ratio a:b, the other being the consequent.
Previous principles, conduct, history, etc.
Earlier, either in time or in order.
senses.example: an antecedent cause

senses.definition: Presumptive.
senses.example: an antecedent improbability

core.definition: Something that came earlier and often caused or explains something that follows it, or the earlier term a pronoun refers to.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on SEE, and the first syllable is 'an' with a reduced vowel. The last syllable is 'dent,' not 'dint,' and the middle sounds like 'tuh.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise word that does not express judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use antecedent in writing and formal conversation, especially in academic, legal, and technical settings. In grammar class it means the noun a pronoun refers to. In everyday speech, people usually say 'the cause' or 'the earlier event.' It is not casual, so use it when you need precision.

distinctions.note: A precedent is a previous case or action that serves as an example, often in law. An antecedent is an earlier condition or cause, not necessarily a model to follow.
A cause directly produces an effect. An antecedent may precede something without causing it, so it is a broader term.

examples.everyday: Bad weather was the antecedent to the traffic jam, so we just waited it out.
examples.professional: Before we retrain the model, let's check which antecedent conditions in the data led to the drift.
examples.analytical: In a conditional 'if p, then q,' p is the antecedent and q is the consequent.

nuance.analogy: Like the first domino in a row: it comes before the others and sets up what follows.
nuance.etymology: From Latin antecedere, 'to go before,' from ante 'before' and cedere 'to go.'
common_mistakes: Using antecedent as a verb, when the verb is antecede, which is rare.
Confusing antecedent with precedent in legal writing.
Misspelling it as antecedant.

antecedent.etymology: From Middle English *antecedent*, borrowed from Old French *antecedent*, from Latin *antecēdēns* (“going before”), from *antecēdō* (“to precede; excel; surpass”).

senses.definition: A Seleucid military commander who led forces against Judas Maccabeus and was killed by him, as described in 1 Maccabees 3.

core.definition: A Seleucid military commander who led forces against Judas Maccabeus and was killed by him, as described in 1 Maccabees 3.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on LOH, with a lighter stress on the first syllable, AP. The ending '-ius' is usually said as 'ee-us' in American English, not 'ee-oos'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a name from history and scripture rather than an evaluative word.
nuance.usage_note: Americans encounter this name mainly in Bible study, seminary, or history classes about the Maccabean period. Since Apollonius is also a common name, people may ask which one you mean, such as Apollonius of Tyana or Apollonius of Rhodes. In casual talk, you would simply say 'the general Apollonius in 1 Maccabees' to specify him.

distinctions.note: Apollos is a different person, a Christian teacher in Acts and 1 Corinthians, and his name is a short form of Apollonius.
Apollo is the Greek god of music and light, or the NASA program; Apollonius is a human name derived from that god's name.

examples.everyday: Our Bible study spent the whole evening on Apollonius, a Greek general in 1 Maccabees, and nobody had heard of him before.
examples.professional: In the seminar paper, I'd cite the battle with Apollonius in 1 Maccabees as evidence of Judas's early tactics against a larger army.
examples.analytical: The commander Apollonius appears in 1 Maccabees as the first enemy officer Judas defeats, a scene that frames the revolt as a victory over imperial power.

nuance.analogy: Like a minor character in a long novel: he appears briefly, but his defeat marks an important turning point in the story.
nuance.etymology: From Greek Apollōnios, a personal name derived from Apollō, the god Apollo.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, as in AP-uh-LOH-nee-us, or saying 'ap-uh-LOH-nee-oos'.
Confusing him with Apollos, the Christian teacher in Acts, who is a different person.
nuance.biblical_note: Apollonius is a name in the Greek Apocrypha, not in the Protestant canon. In 1 Maccabees 3:10-12, Apollonius, a Seleucid commander, leads an army against Israel, and Judas Maccabeus defeats him and kills him, then takes his sword. In 2 Maccabees 3:5-7, a different Apollonius, son of Thraseas, is governor of Coele-Syria and Phoenicia and becomes involved in a dispute over the Temple treasury. These passages show the Seleucid pressure on Judea that led to the Maccabean revolt.

senses.definition: The fact or action of becoming or making into a god; deification.
Glorification, exaltation; crediting someone or something with extraordinary power or status.
senses.example: The turn of the century saw the apotheosis of digital technology.

senses.definition: A glorified example or ideal; the apex or pinnacle (of a concept or belief).
The best moment or highest point in the development of something, for example of a life or career; the apex, culmination, or climax (of a development).
senses.example: The apotheosis of her career was her appointment as chairman.

senses.definition: Release from earthly life, ascension to heaven; death.
The latent entity that mediates between a person's psyche and their thoughts. The id, ego and superego in Freudian Psychology are examples of this.

core.definition: The highest or most perfect example of something, or the act of raising a person to godlike status.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on OH, the third syllable. The th is voiceless, as in 'thin', and the ending is 'sis', like 'crisis', not '-us'.

nuance.connotation: Positive, since it usually means a glorious peak; it can sound grand or slightly ironic when used for something minor.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it for a peak moment, often in writing about sports, art, or business, as in 'the concert was the apotheosis of her career.' It is formal and a bit grand, so in casual speech peak, high point, or best moment sounds more natural.

distinctions.note: Peak is plain and neutral; apotheosis suggests an almost sacred or glorified climax.
Deification means making someone a god; apotheosis can mean that literally or the figurative pinnacle.

examples.everyday: For me, that summer concert was the apotheosis of the whole season.
examples.professional: The product launch was the apotheosis of eighteen months of cross-team work.
examples.analytical: Romantic critics treated the poet's late work as the apotheosis of genius, a transcendence beyond mere craft.

nuance.analogy: Like a mountain climb that reaches its summit, where the whole path seems to rise to a single point.
nuance.etymology: From Greek apotheōsis, deification, from apotheoun, to make a god of.
common_mistakes: Using it for any good event; it implies a peak of glory, not just a pleasant moment.
Mispronouncing the th as an s sound, as in 'uh-pah-SEE-oh-sis'.

apotheosis.etymology: Latin *apotheōsis*, from Ancient Greek *ἀποθέωσις*, from verb *ἀποθεόω* (“deify”) (factitive verb formed from *θεός* (“God”) with intensive prefix *ἀπο-*) + *-σις* (“forms noun of action”).

senses.definition: The state or action of desiring or craving.

core.definition: A strong desire or craving for something, especially a natural inclination toward a particular thing or experience.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the middle vowels reduce to a short 'ih' and schwa. The ending '-ence' is pronounced 'uns', not 'ens' with a clear 'e'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly positive. It describes a natural drive, often for knowledge or experience.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'appetence' in speech and see it mostly in older philosophy, literature, or formal writing. In everyday English people say 'appetite', 'craving', or 'hunger for' something. Use it when you want a learned or precise word for a deep natural inclination.

distinctions.note: Appetite is the common word for hunger or a general desire, while appetence is a more formal word for a natural inclination.
Craving suggests an intense, often urgent need, while appetence describes a steadier, more natural drive.
Aspiration is a goal you work toward, while appetence is a desire or pull that exists before any goal is set.

examples.everyday: She has a real appetence for adventure; she'd go hiking every weekend if she could.
examples.professional: The hiring manager praised her appetence for hard problems, which is exactly what this team needs.
examples.analytical: Aristotle's account of human appetence shows how desire is directed toward goods that the soul perceives as good.

nuance.analogy: Like a magnet's steady pull toward metal, which is natural and constant rather than sudden.
nuance.etymology: From Latin appetentia, from appetere, 'to strive after', from ad- 'to' plus petere, 'to seek'.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'appetence' with 'appetite' and using them as interchangeable in everyday speech.
Stressing the second syllable, as in 'uh-PET-uns'.
Pronouncing the ending with a clear 'ence' sound instead of 'uns'.

appetence.etymology: Circa 1600, from French *appétence*, from Latin *appetentia*, from *appetere* (“to seek after”).

senses.definition: A protective layer over a body, vehicle, or other object intended to deflect or diffuse damaging forces.
senses.example: a suit of armor

senses.definition: A natural form of this kind of protection on an animal's body.
A metal plate, protecting a ship, military vehicle, or aircraft.
A tank, or other heavy mobile assault vehicle.
The naturally occurring surface of pebbles, rocks or boulders that line the bed of a waterway or beach and provide protection against erosion.
A military formation consisting primarily of tanks or other armored fighting vehicles, collectively.
To equip something with armor or a protective coating or hardening.
To provide something with an analogous form of protection.

core.definition: A protective covering, such as metal plates or a padded vest, worn or fitted to shield a person, animal, or vehicle from attack.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the second is an unstressed r-colored vowel. Say AR-mer with a clear r and no separate 'oh' sound. The American spelling is armor; the British armour is pronounced the same.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: it suggests safety and protection, and figuratively it can mean emotional self-defense.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use armor for protective gear in sports, police and military work, and vehicles, and figuratively for emotional defenses, as in 'emotional armor.' Spell it armor, never armour, which is British. Body armor is the common term for a bulletproof vest, and armored vehicle is the usual term for a military vehicle with metal plating.

distinctions.note: Armament means weapons or the arming of forces, while armor is the protective covering that defends against weapons.
A shield is carried or held up to block blows, while armor is worn or built into the object it protects.

examples.everyday: My brother bought body armor for his security job, and he says the vest is heavy in the summer.
examples.professional: Our procurement team needs quotes for armor plating on the new transport vehicles by Friday.
examples.analytical: Many people build emotional armor after betrayal, and the armor that protects them can also keep out the love they need.

nuance.analogy: Armor works like a turtle's shell: a hard outer layer that deflects what would otherwise reach the soft body inside.
nuance.etymology: From Old French armure, from Latin armatura and arma, meaning weapons or equipment.
common_mistakes: Writing armour, the British spelling, in American writing.
Using armor to mean the place where weapons are kept; that place is an armory.
nuance.biblical_note: Armor appears in the Bible as soldiers' equipment and as a spiritual image. In 1 Samuel 17:38 Saul dresses David in his own armor before David faces Goliath, and David sets it aside. Romans 13:12 tells believers to put on the armor of light, and Ephesians 6:11 tells them to put on the whole armor of God to stand against the schemes of the devil. The Greek word panoplia in Ephesians 6:11 means a full set of armor, and hopla in Romans 13:12 means weapons or armor.

armor.etymology: From Middle English *armure*, *armour*, *armor*, *armeure*, borrowed from Anglo-Norman *armure* and Old French *armeüre*, from Latin *armātūra*.

senses.definition: To officially charge someone in a court of law.
senses.example: He was arraigned in Washington, D.C., on the 25th of that month on charges of treason.

senses.definition: To call to account, or accuse, before the bar of reason, taste, or any other tribunal.
Arraignment.

core.definition: To bring a person before a court to be formally charged with a crime and asked to plead.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on RAIN, the second syllable. The first syllable is a weak schwa, and the r is clearly pronounced. Do not confuse it with 'arrange,' which ends in a j sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and legal. It describes a serious formal step, so it can sound grim in news stories.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use arraign almost only in legal and news contexts, like 'He was arraigned on Monday.' In everyday talk, say 'charged' or 'going to court.' The verb usually appears in the passive form. You would rarely use it for a personal complaint, though some writers use it figuratively.

distinctions.note: To indict is for a grand jury to formally charge someone; arraign is the later court step where the charges are read and the defendant pleads.
Charge is a general word for accusing someone of a crime; arraign describes the formal court appearance.
Accuse is informal and can be private; arraign is a formal legal action taken in court.

examples.everyday: I heard he was arraigned this morning on the shoplifting charge.
examples.professional: Our compliance lawyer said the company won't be arraigned, since this is a civil dispute and no criminal charges were filed.
examples.analytical: A court arraigns a defendant to make the charge public and to require a plea before the case can move forward.

nuance.analogy: Arraigning someone is like calling their name in court: the charge is announced, and they must respond.
nuance.etymology: From Old French araisnier, 'to call to account,' from Latin ad- and rationare, 'to reason'.
common_mistakes: Confusing arraign with arrange, which has a different meaning and ending
Using arraign for a private accusation or complaint, when accuse is correct
Saying 'arraigned for' without naming the charge; American usage is 'arraigned on charges of'

arraign.etymology: From Middle English *areynen* (“to interrogate, arraign, reprimand”), from Anglo-Norman *areiner*, *arener*, from Old French *araisnier*, *areisnier*, *aresnier* (“to speak to, address; accuse”), from Vulgar Latin **arratiōnāre*, from Latin *adratiōnāre*,…

senses.definition: A joint or the collection of joints at which something is articulated, or hinged, for bending.
senses.example: The articulation allowed the robot to move around corners.

senses.definition: A manner or method by which elements of a system are connected.
The quality, clarity, or sharpness of speech; the movement within the mouth that allows for those things.
senses.example: His volume is reasonable, but his articulation could use work.

senses.definition: The mechanism by which a sound is formed in the vocal tract.
senses.example: manner of articulation

senses.definition: The interrelation and congruence of the flow of data between financial statements of an entity, especially between the income statement and balance sheet.
The induction of a pupil into a new school or college.
Such a joint in an animalian body, as for example between bones or between exoskeleton segments.
The manner in which a note is attacked.
senses.example: The articulation in this piece is tricky because it alternates between legato and staccato.

core.definition: The clarity and precision of speech, or the way the mouth, tongue, and lips shape sounds to form words.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on LAY, the syllable before -shun, while the first syllable has only secondary stress. Say the -tion ending as 'shun,' not 'tee-on,' and keep the 'cu' as a quick 'yuh.'

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. Praising someone's articulation means they speak or write clearly and precisely; it is rarely negative.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use articulation to praise a speaker or writer who expresses ideas clearly, as in 'She has great articulation.' In everyday talk, 'You explain things really clearly' sounds more natural. The term is common in reviews, interviews, speech therapy, and academic evaluations, where it sounds polite and professional.

distinctions.note: Pronunciation is how a word is said correctly; articulation is the clarity and precision with which sounds and ideas are expressed.
Fluency is speed and smoothness of speech; articulation is clarity, so a speaker can be fluent yet unclear.
Eloquence adds persuasive power and style; articulation simply means being clear and precise.

examples.everyday: Your sister has great articulation, so I could understand every word of her toast.
examples.professional: Her articulation of the project risks in the status meeting was clear enough that the whole team agreed on next steps.
examples.analytical: Rawls's articulation of justice as fairness rests on a precise distinction between principles of justice and the institutions they govern.

nuance.analogy: Good articulation is like a clean lens: the ideas pass through without distortion.
nuance.etymology: From Latin articulatio, from articulare 'to divide into joints', from articulus 'small joint'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in 'AR-tik-yoo-lay-shun'; keep the main stress on LAY.
Using articulation as a verb or adjective; the verb is articulate and the adjective is articulate or articulated.

articulation.etymology: From Middle English *articulacioun*, from Old French *articulacion*, from Medieval Latin *articulatio*.

senses.definition: The act, or an instance, of ascribing a quality, characteristic, quotation, artistic work, or other thing to someone or something.
The stratification of people according to inborn characteristics (such as race or sex) outside of their control.

core.definition: The act of attributing a quality, quotation, artwork, or cause to a particular person or thing.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, SKRIP, and the ending is a quick shun. Do not pronounce the first syllable as ass, since the word begins with a weak uh.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a technical term for attribution and carries no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ascription mostly in scholarly writing, art history, literary studies, and philosophy. In everyday talk they say attribution or credit. If you hear ascription in a meeting, the speaker is usually being precise or academic.

distinctions.note: Attribution is the common term in art, journalism, and quotation, while ascription is more formal and abstract.
Assignment means giving someone a task or role; ascription means crediting a quality or work to a source.

examples.everyday: I'd be careful about the ascription of that quote to Einstein, because it probably isn't his.
examples.professional: The ascription of the bug to the new library was wrong, since the logs point to our own code.
examples.analytical: The ascription of mental states to other people is central to debates about theory of mind.

nuance.analogy: Ascription is like a label placed on a jar, telling you what it contains and where it came from.
nuance.etymology: From Latin ascriptio, from ascribere, meaning to write in addition.
common_mistakes: Using ascription in casual conversation where attribution would sound more natural.
Stressing the wrong syllable, saying uh-SKRIP-tion instead of uh-SKRIP-shun.

senses.definition: The district within which a bailie or bailiff has jurisdiction.
senses.example: The Bailiwick of Jersey.

senses.definition: A person's concern or sphere of operations, their area of skill or authority.

core.definition: A person's area of expertise, responsibility, or control, often used in a humorous or informal way.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final syllable rhymes with 'quick' and 'trick', not 'week'. The middle syllable is a reduced vowel, so it sounds like 'lih'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly playful. It is used to describe someone's domain, often with a light, self-aware tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use bailiwick mostly in writing, speeches, and polished conversation, usually with a bit of humor. You might say 'Taxes are not my bailiwick' when you want to politely admit that a topic is outside your expertise. It is less common in casual speech, where people often say 'that's not my thing' or 'that's not my area.'

distinctions.note: Jurisdiction is a formal term for legal authority, while bailiwick is looser and can refer to any area of skill or responsibility.
A specialty is a field of knowledge or practice, while bailiwick can describe the area someone controls or cares about, with a more personal or humorous tone.

collocations: a matter for the finance bailiwick

examples.everyday: Don't ask me to fix your car, because mechanics are outside my bailiwick.
examples.professional: Model governance falls within the risk team's bailiwick, so you should send that question to them.
examples.analytical: Philosophy has long claimed the bailiwick of conceptual analysis, though empirical scientists increasingly contest that boundary.

nuance.analogy: A bailiwick is like a kitchen in a house: each person has a part they run, and others don't walk in and rearrange things.
nuance.etymology: From bailie (an official who governed a district) plus wick, meaning a district or dwelling, from Old English wīc.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the last syllable as 'week', which is incorrect.
Using bailiwick for any hobby, when it usually refers to a field of responsibility or expertise.

senses.definition: A field, stadium or park where ball, especially baseball, is played.
The general vicinity; somewhere close; a broad approximation.
senses.example: Let’s get in the ballpark, then worry about the fine details.

senses.definition: Approximate; close; on the right order of magnitude.
To make a rough estimate of.
senses.example: If you don’t have the exact expense total, just ballpark it.

core.definition: A rough range or general area that something falls within; an approximate size, amount or estimate.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on BALL, and the word is pronounced as one compound with a clear r in park. Do not say pork or pawk; the R is pronounced in American speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It signals that a number or idea is approximate, which is useful in meetings but can sound casual in formal writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ballpark constantly in business and everyday talk, especially in the phrase in the ballpark, meaning roughly correct. A common request is Can you give me a ballpark? and a natural reply is Ballpark is fine, or Somewhere around ten thousand. It is informal, so in a formal report you would more likely write approximate or estimated.

distinctions.note: Estimate is more neutral and formal, while ballpark stresses that the number is rough and not precise.
Exact figure means a precise number, which is the opposite of a ballpark.
Guesstimate is more humorous and informal, and it suggests a guess with little basis.

examples.everyday: Roughly how much do you think the wedding will cost? Just give me a ballpark.
examples.professional: Can you give me a ballpark on the migration timeline before the steering meeting on Thursday?
examples.analytical: The estimate is only ballpark, but it is enough to show that the proposal is economically plausible.

nuance.analogy: A ballpark is the big field where you know roughly where the game is happening, even without seeing each play.
nuance.etymology: From the baseball ballpark, the stadium; the figurative sense of roughly or approximately developed in twentieth-century American English.
common_mistakes: Writing ball park as two words in formal writing; ballpark is the standard form.
Stressing park too strongly; the main stress is on ball.
Using ballpark as a precise term, which contradicts its meaning of approximate.

conversation.text: Can you ballpark how many hours this will take?
I don't need exact numbers, just a ballpark.
"What will it cost?" "I'd say somewhere in the ballpark of fifty grand."

senses.definition: Sensational or clamorous advertising or publicity.
Noisy shouting or uproar.
Certain species in family Hemiramphidae, inshore, surface-dwelling needlefish forming sizeable schools.
Hemiramphus brasiliensis.
An unseaworthy or slovenly ship.
To sensationalize or make grand claims.

core.definition: Loud, exaggerated publicity or hype designed to attract attention, often for a product, event or movie.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on the last syllable, HOO, which rhymes with too. Do not stress the first syllable or pronounce the last syllable as how.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests overstatement and hype, so it is usually used to criticize publicity rather than praise it.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ballyhoo to criticize big marketing campaigns, movie launches or media coverage that seems excessive. A natural comment is All that ballyhoo for a phone that looks the same as the last one. It is informal and somewhat old-fashioned, so it is more common in conversation and journalism than in formal writing.

distinctions.note: Hype is the more common modern word for exaggerated promotion, and it is equally negative.
Publicity is neutral and can be accurate, while ballyhoo implies excessive and noisy promotion.
Fanfare describes a celebratory display, often positive, while ballyhoo suggests overhyped noise.

examples.everyday: All that ballyhoo about the new phone, and it looks exactly like the old one.
examples.professional: The product launch got a lot of ballyhoo, but the actual adoption numbers after three months were modest.
examples.analytical: Much of the ballyhoo surrounding the theory conceals how little empirical evidence supports its central claims.

nuance.analogy: Ballyhoo is like a carnival barker shouting loudly to draw a crowd, even when the show is ordinary.
nuance.etymology: Origin uncertain; first recorded in American English in the early twentieth century.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in BAL-ee-hoo; the main stress is on the final syllable.
Using ballyhoo as a neutral or positive word of praise; it normally suggests overstatement.
Pronouncing the last syllable like how instead of hoo.

senses.definition: A great and mighty beast which God shows to Job in Job 40:15–24.
Any great and mighty monster.
Something which has the qualities of great power and might, and monstrous proportions.

core.definition: Something enormous and powerful, such as a huge company, machine, or creature with overwhelming size and strength.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on HEE, the second syllable. The final 'th' is unvoiced, like the th in 'with,' and the middle syllable is a reduced 'muh.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It emphasizes enormous size and dominance, and it can suggest a clumsy or intimidating presence.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use behemoth for giant companies, buildings, or vehicles, often in business and tech news, such as 'a retail behemoth.' It is more vivid than 'giant' and sounds somewhat dramatic. A natural casual reply to 'That company is a behemoth' is 'Yeah, they basically run the whole market.'

distinctions.note: Giant is a general word for something very large, while behemoth stresses overwhelming power and monstrous size.
Colossus suggests something massive and towering, often a symbol of power, while behemoth suggests a huge and sometimes unwieldy force.

examples.everyday: That big-box store is a behemoth, you can spend an hour just looking for the bathroom.
examples.professional: The cloud provider is a behemoth, so migrating to it means negotiating a contract with terms we cannot easily change.
examples.analytical: The modern state can resemble a behemoth whose size enables both protection and a dangerous indifference to individuals.

nuance.analogy: A behemoth is like a freight train: enormously powerful, hard to stop, and slow to turn.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew behemoth, the plural of behemah 'beast', the great creature described in the Book of Job.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as 'BEE-hi-moth' with the stress on the first syllable.
Using it for anything merely big, when it suggests overwhelming power or monstrous scale.

behemoth.etymology: From Middle English *behemoth,bemoth*, from Late Latin *behemoth*, from Hebrew *בְּהֵמוֹת*.

senses.definition: Obligated to provide, display, or do something for another; indebted, obliged for a bounden duty.
senses.example: From an early age, I had decided I wanted to be beholden to no one.

core.definition: Feeling obligated to someone because they helped you, so that you owe them gratitude or loyalty and may feel less free.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on HOHL, and the final syllable is a reduced 'dun' with a schwa vowel. The 'l' is clearly pronounced in American English, unlike some British speakers who may soften it.

nuance.connotation: Often neutral, but it can be negative because it suggests losing independence to someone who has power or money. It can also be a warm way to express thanks.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use beholden most often in politics, business, and formal writing, as in 'beholden to donors.' In everyday speech, people sometimes say 'I'm beholden to you' to thank someone warmly. A natural reply to that is 'Oh, don't mention it, I was happy to help.'

distinctions.note: Obligated describes a general duty, while beholden implies gratitude or dependence that can limit your independence.
Indebted can mean grateful for help or owing money, while beholden emphasizes dependence on someone's favor or influence.

examples.everyday: I'm beholden to you for watching the kids last night, so let me buy you dinner this week.
examples.professional: Our consultants aren't beholden to any vendor, so their recommendations are unbiased.
examples.analytical: A judge who is beholden to the executive branch cannot fully serve as an impartial check on its power.

nuance.analogy: Being beholden is like carrying an unpaid favor in your pocket: it is not a debt of money, but it shapes what you can freely say.
nuance.etymology: Past participle of archaic behold in the sense 'to hold,' from Old English behealdan, meaning to keep or hold.
common_mistakes: Confusing beholden with behold, the verb meaning to look at something.
Using beholden for a mild duty, when it usually suggests gratitude or a dependence that limits freedom.

beholden.etymology: From Middle English *biholden* (“beholden, obligated”), past participle of *biholden* (“to behold, look at”), though that verb does not mean "to bind, obligate".

senses.definition: To give a false representation of.
senses.example: Her smooth complexion and dark hair belie her actual age.

senses.definition: To contradict, to show (something) to be false.
senses.example: Her obvious nervousness belied what she said.

senses.definition: To lie around; encompass.
To call a liar; to accuse of falsehood.
To fill with lies; to lie to.

core.definition: To show that appearances or claims are false, or to give a misleading impression of something.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the only syllable, which is a diphthong that sounds like 'eye'. Do not confuse it with 'belly' or 'bee-lie'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It suggests a gap between appearance and reality, often a surprising one, and is used when evidence shows something to be false.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it in writing and serious speech, as in 'His calm voice belied his anger' or 'The numbers belie the claim.' It is rarely casual; in speech, 'doesn't match' or 'contradicts' is simpler. It is common in journalism, reviews, and analysis.

distinctions.note: Contradict is direct and neutral about what is said; belie focuses on how appearance or evidence misrepresents reality.
Deny means saying something is not true; belie shows through evidence or behavior that something is false.

examples.everyday: She looks relaxed, but her shaky hands belie how nervous she really is.
examples.professional: The usage numbers belie the claim that the feature is popular, since most users tried it once and left.
examples.analytical: The poem's calm surface belies a deep anxiety about loss, which the repeated images of closed doors make clear.

nuance.analogy: Like a calm lake hiding a strong current beneath the surface.
nuance.etymology: From Old English beleogan, 'to lie about, deceive', from be- and lie.
common_mistakes: Confusing belie with lie or belay; belie means to show as false, not to tell a lie.
Adding a preposition, as in 'belie to' or 'belie of'; the verb takes a direct object.

belie.etymology: From Middle English *belyen*, *beliggen*, from Old English *beliċġan*, *biliċġan* (“to lie around, surround, hedge in, encompass”), from **biliggjan*, from Proto-Germanic **biligjaną* (“to lie around”).

senses.definition: The quality of being benighted.

core.definition: The state of being benighted; a lack of education, knowledge, or enlightenment.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the NY syllable, and reduce the -ed to 'id' and the final -ness to 'nes'. Avoid pronouncing the -ed as a separate 'ed' syllable.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes intellectual or cultural darkness, and it sounds judgmental.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this noun; it appears in literary criticism, history, or formal essays. In everyday talk they would say ignorance or lack of education. It is best reserved for writing about a broad cultural or intellectual condition.

distinctions.note: Ignorance is a common everyday word for lacking knowledge, while benightedness is literary and suggests a deeper cultural darkness.
Superstition names a specific false belief, while benightedness describes a general state of unenlightenment.

examples.everyday: I used to think small towns were full of benightedness, but my neighbors are some of the smartest people I know.
examples.professional: The benightedness of our old approval process meant that every change waited weeks for a signature.
examples.analytical: Kant's essay on enlightenment describes benightedness as a self-imposed immaturity, a failure to use one's own understanding.

nuance.analogy: Benightedness is like a windowless room: no light gets in, so no one knows what is on the shelves.
nuance.etymology: From benighted with the noun suffix -ness.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the -ed as a full extra syllable.
Using benightedness for a single missing fact; ignorance is more natural for that.

senses.definition: Town in the book of Judith, besieged by the Assyrian general Holofernes and saved by the widow Judith.

core.definition: Town in the book of Judith, besieged by the Assyrian general Holofernes and saved by the widow Judith.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, THOO, and the final syllables are light: 'lee-uh'. The 'th' is voiceless.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in most uses; in religious study it carries the heroic sense of a city saved by faith.
nuance.usage_note: Bethulia is almost always discussed in connection with the book of Judith, which appears in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles and in the Protestant Apocrypha. Americans may use it in Bible study or literary discussions. In casual conversation it is rare, so explain the story if you mention it.

examples.everyday: Did you know the story of Judith is set in a town called Bethulia that was under siege?
examples.professional: The Judith story offers a useful case study for leadership under siege, using the people of Bethulia as the example.
examples.analytical: The rescue of Bethulia by Judith reverses the elders' expectations and shows God working through an unexpected agent.

nuance.analogy: Like a small hilltop town that everyone expects to fall, yet is saved by one brave person.
common_mistakes: Confusing Bethulia with Bethlehem or Bethel.
Assuming Bethulia is a well-known historical town; its exact location is uncertain.
nuance.biblical_note: Bethulia is the town in the book of Judith, which is in the Catholic and Orthodox Old Testaments and in the Protestant Apocrypha. Judith 7 describes the siege, the water shortage and the despair of the elders. Judith 8 records Judith's prayer and her plan. Judith 13 reports the death of Holofernes and the deliverance of the town.

senses.definition: To grow or become white.
senses.example: His cheek blanched with fear.

senses.definition: To take the color out of, and make white; to bleach.
senses.example: to blanch linen

senses.definition: To cook by dipping briefly into boiling water, then directly into cold water.
To whiten, for example the surface of meat, by plunging into boiling water and afterwards into cold, so as to harden the surface and retain the juices.
To bleach by excluding light, for example the stalks or leaves of plants by earthing them up or tying them together.
To make white by removing the skin of, for example by scalding.
senses.example: to blanch almonds

senses.definition: To give a white luster to (silver, before stamping, in the process of coining)
To cover (sheet iron) with a coating of tin.
To give a favorable appearance to; to whitewash; to whiten;
To avoid, as from fear; to evade; to leave unnoticed.
To cause to turn aside or back.
senses.example: to blanch a deer

senses.definition: To use evasion.

core.definition: To turn suddenly pale, as from fear, shock or illness; or to briefly boil food, then chill it.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the only syllable, and the vowel is the short a of 'cat'. Pronounce it like 'branch' with a 'bl' start; the ch is the sound of 'church'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. The pale sense suggests fear, shock or sickness; the cooking sense is neutral and practical.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say blanch when someone goes pale from shock, as in 'he blanched at the bill'. In the kitchen, blanch means putting vegetables or almonds into boiling water for a short time and then into ice water, which is common in recipes. The verb is more often written than spoken in everyday talk, so you might hear 'went pale' in casual speech.

distinctions.note: Pale is a common everyday adjective for a light or ill complexion; blanch is a verb describing the sudden moment of losing color.
Bleach means to make something white or lighter with chemicals; blanch is more about a sudden change in a person's face or a brief cooking step.

examples.everyday: When I told my roommate the rent went up, she blanched and asked if I was joking.
examples.professional: Before we commit to the new vendor, the finance lead blanched at the license fee and asked for a discount.
examples.analytical: Her argument shows how fear can make a listener blanch, even before the evidence has been fully weighed.

nuance.analogy: Like a photo that loses its color in strong light, leaving only pale outlines.
nuance.etymology: From Old French blanchir, 'to make white', from blanc, 'white'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the ch as 'sh', making it sound like 'blansh'.
Confusing blanch with blench, which is a different and rare word meaning to flinch.

blanch.etymology: From Middle English *blaunchen*, from Old French *blanchir*, from Old French *blanc* (“white”), from *blancus*, from **blank*, from Proto-Germanic **blankaz* (“bright, shining, blinding, white”), from Proto-Indo-European **bʰleyǵ-* (“to shine”).

senses.definition: An act of bluffing; a false expression of the strength of one’s position in order to intimidate or deceive; braggadocio.
senses.example: That is only bluff, or That is only a bluff.

senses.definition: An attempt to represent oneself as holding a stronger hand than one actually does.
senses.example: John’s bet was a bluff: he bet without even so much as a pair.

senses.definition: One who bluffs; a bluffer.
A high, steep bank, for example by a river or the sea, or beside a ravine or plain; a cliff with a broad face.
A small wood or stand of trees, typically poplar or willow.
The card game poker.
Pretense, excuse.
To make a bluff; to give the impression that one’s hand is stronger than it is.
senses.example: John bluffed by betting without even a pair.

senses.definition: To frighten, deter, or deceive with a false show of strength or confidence; to give a false impression of strength or temerity in order to intimidate or gain some advantage.
senses.example: The government claims it will call an election if this bill does not pass. Is it truly ready to do so, or is it bluffing?

senses.definition: To perform or achieve by bluffing.
senses.example: We bluffed our way past the guards.

senses.definition: To give false information intentionally, to lie (to someone), to deceive; to put on an act.
To fluff, puff or swell up.
Having a broad, flattened front.
senses.example: the bluff bows of a ship

senses.definition: Rising steeply with a flat or rounded front.
Surly; churlish; gruff; rough.
Roughly frank and hearty in one's manners.
senses.example: a bluff answer

core.definition: To pretend you are stronger or more confident than you really are, usually to scare someone or get what you want.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the single syllable and keep the vowel short, like the u in "but". Do not add an extra vowel, and do not confuse it with "bluff" meaning a high cliff, which uses the same sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative to neutral. It suggests deception or bragging, although a bluff in negotiation or poker is considered a normal strategic move.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use bluff most often in poker, negotiations, and arguments, as in "He's just bluffing." The phrase "call your bluff" means to challenge someone to prove a claim is real, and a natural reply is "Okay, let's see." Saying someone is bluffing in a friendly way is common, but accusing a colleague of bluffing in a meeting can sound hostile.

distinctions.note: Pretend is a general word for acting as if something is true; bluff specifically means projecting false strength or confidence to influence others.
A lie is a false statement; a bluff can involve no spoken falsehood at all, only a confident pose or action.
Threaten means to warn of harm, usually sincerely; a bluff is a threat or claim that the speaker does not intend to carry out.

examples.everyday: Don't worry about him, he's just bluffing about quitting his job.
examples.professional: The vendor was bluffing about having another buyer, so we asked for a better price and got it.
examples.analytical: Bluff depends on the asymmetry of information: the bluffer succeeds only when the opponent cannot verify the claimed strength.

nuance.analogy: A bluff is like a shop window display of a strong product that is actually empty inside; it looks good until someone checks.
nuance.etymology: From Dutch bluffen, to brag or boast; the card-game sense developed later.
common_mistakes: Using bluff for an honest mistake or exaggeration rather than a deliberate deception.
Saying "bluff the bill" or similar with wrong prepositions; the usual phrases are "bluff your way through" and "call someone's bluff."

bluff.etymology: Probably from Dutch *bluffen* (“to brag”), from Middle Dutch *bluffen* (“to make something swell; to bluff”); or from the noun *bluf* (“bragging”).

senses.definition: Having a thick edge or point; not sharp.
Dull in understanding; slow of discernment; opposed to acute.
Abrupt in address; plain; unceremonious; wanting in the forms of civility; rough in manners or speech.
senses.example: I was taken aback by the blunt admission that he had never liked my company.

senses.definition: Hard to impress or penetrate.
Slow or deficient in feeling: insensitive.
A fencer's practice foil with a soft tip.
A short needle with a strong point.
A marijuana cigar.
Money.
A playboating move resembling a cartwheel performed on a wave.
To dull the edge or point of, by making it thicker; to make blunt.
To repress or weaken; to impair the force, keenness, or susceptibility, of.
senses.example: It blunted my appetite.

core.definition: Speaking or acting in a very direct, honest way, without trying to soften the message or be polite.

pronunciation.tip: Pronounce it as one syllable with a short u and a clear final t. Do not add an extra t sound in the middle of the consonant cluster.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It can be admired as honesty, but it may sound rude if used without tact.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often use blunt to describe someone who gives frank feedback, as in "To be blunt, the report is late." The phrase "to be blunt" is a common way to warn that bad news is coming. Calling someone blunt is usually a mild criticism, while saying "I'll be honest" is a softer alternative in most workplaces.

distinctions.note: Direct is usually neutral or positive and focuses on clarity; blunt can suggest a lack of tact or warmth.
Frank is more positive, implying honest openness; blunt can suggest harshness.
Rude implies intent to offend; blunt describes frankness that may or may not be meant to hurt.

examples.everyday: I'll be blunt with you, the tacos were too salty.
examples.professional: I want to be blunt about the timeline: the launch will slip if we do not cut scope this week.
examples.analytical: A blunt argument can be valuable in philosophy because it removes rhetorical cushioning, but it can also obscure nuance.

nuance.analogy: Blunt speech is like a plain cardboard box: it does the job clearly, with no decoration.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English blunt, origin uncertain.
common_mistakes: Using blunt to mean "stupid," which is an older sense and sounds odd in modern English.
Confusing blunt with dull for objects; a dull knife is blunt, but a blunt person is not necessarily dull-witted.

blunt.etymology: From Middle English *blunt*, *blont*, from Old English **blunt*, probably of origin, possibly related to, related to *blind* >.

senses.definition: To boil to such an extent as to overflow its container.
senses.example: I forgot about the rice and it boiled over.

senses.definition: To reach the point where aggressive action is taken.
To act aggressively angry.
senses.example: He boiled over all night.

senses.definition: To buck aggressively.
senses.example: The stallion boiled over, throwing Robert from her back.

core.definition: To overflow while boiling, or to suddenly erupt in anger, violence, or strong emotion after building up.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on 'OH' in 'over,' and the final syllable is a rhotic, reduced 'ur' sound. Do not add a 't' sound to 'over,' since it is a flap-free 'v' sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It usually describes conflict, frustration, or anger reaching an uncontrolled point.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use boil over for a pot spilling on the stove and, figuratively, for tensions or anger that suddenly burst out, as in 'Tensions boiled over at the meeting.' It is common in news and everyday conversation. A natural reply is often a sympathetic comment, such as 'I can see why things got heated.'

distinctions.note: Explode suggests a sudden, violent release, while boil over suggests a buildup of pressure or emotion that eventually spills out.
Flare up describes a sudden but usually brief outburst, while boil over suggests a longer buildup before the eruption.

collocations: anger boiled over at the meeting

examples.everyday: The pot boiled over while I was answering the phone, so there's pasta water all over the stove.
examples.professional: Tensions boiled over during the review when two teams argued about the release schedule.
examples.analytical: Years of unresolved grievances boiled over into open protest, which revealed how long the pressure had been building.

nuance.analogy: Like a pot left on high heat too long, a person or group can build up pressure until it spills over.
nuance.etymology: Boil plus over; the literal kitchen sense of overflowing gave rise to the figurative sense of emotion breaking out.
common_mistakes: Using it transitively, as in 'boil over the pot,' which is incorrect.
Confusing it with 'boil down,' which means reducing to the main point.

conversation.text: Watch the pasta so it doesn't boil over.
The milk boiled over and made a mess.
The argument boiled over at dinner.

senses.definition: To cause someone to remember something from the past.
senses.example: The smell of the magnolia brought back sweet memories of my childhood.

senses.definition: To fetch something.
senses.example: I brought back the groceries.

senses.definition: To reenact an old rule or law.
senses.example: In the UK it is customary to hold a vote every few years on whether to bring back the death penalty.

senses.definition: To revive, to resurrect; to cause something dead to be alive once again.

core.definition: To return something to a place or person, or to remind someone of the past, or to revive an old custom.

pronunciation.tip: In phrasal verbs the particle takes the stress, so stress 'back', not 'bring'. In speech, 'bring it back' links smoothly into roughly 'bri-ni-BAK'. Keep the ng sound clear.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, but it can be positive when it means reviving something good, such as a memory, or negative when it brings back painful memories.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use bring back constantly in everyday life, especially for returning items to a store: 'I need to bring this back to Target.' It is also used for memories ('That song brings back memories') and for reviving old practices ('They want to bring back the old menu'). A natural reply is 'Sure, I'll bring it back tomorrow.'

distinctions.note: Return is more formal and can mean going back yourself, while bring back usually means carrying something back to a place.
Take back can also mean returning items, but it can also mean withdrawing a statement, so bring back is clearer for physical objects.

collocations: bring it back to the store

examples.everyday: Can you bring back the milk when you come home tonight?
examples.professional: We should bring back the old release notes format, because people said they liked it better.
examples.analytical: The essay's nostalgia tries to bring back a lost sense of communal worship that modern life has eroded.

nuance.analogy: Bring back is like pressing rewind: the thing returns to the place or time it came from.
nuance.etymology: Bring comes from Old English bringan; back comes from Old English bæc, meaning 'behind, backward'.
common_mistakes: Stressing 'bring' instead of 'back', which sounds unnatural to Americans.
Using bring back for a person who returned alone; say 'came back' or 'returned' instead.
Confusing it with take back, which can also mean withdrawing a remark.

conversation.text: Can you bring back my charger when you're done with it?
I borrowed his ladder, so I need to bring it back today.
That song really brings back memories of high school.
I hope they bring back the pumpkin muffins this fall.
You can bring it back within thirty days with a receipt.
I brought back the lamp because it didn't match the room.
This song brings back so many memories from college.

senses.definition: Of, or in the manner of a brute.
Bestial; lacking human sensibility.

core.definition: Like a brute animal; crude, coarse, or cruel, with little thought, refinement, or human feeling.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, BROO. The -ish ending is short and unstressed, so do not stretch the u into brew-tish.

nuance.connotation: Negative: it criticizes behavior or conditions as crude, cruel, or uncivilized.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use brutish mostly in writing and formal speech to criticize behavior or living conditions, as in a brutish way to treat workers. In casual speech they usually choose brutal, harsh, or animalistic. A natural response is, that's harsh, but I see your point.

distinctions.note: Brutal describes harsh or violent acts; brutish describes crude, uncivilized behavior or character.
Bestial is stronger and more literal, implying animal cruelty; brutish is a broader insult about lack of refinement.

examples.everyday: That was a brutish way to end the conversation; you could have just said goodbye.
examples.professional: The brutish budget cuts made the team lose its best engineers within a quarter.
examples.analytical: Hobbes described the state of nature as solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short, a claim about human life without society.

nuance.analogy: Like rough stone compared to polished marble: the shape is there, but the finish is missing.
nuance.etymology: From brute plus the suffix -ish, meaning like a brute; brute comes from Latin brutus, meaning heavy or dull.
common_mistakes: Confusing brutish with brutal; brutish is about crude manner, while brutal is about violence or harshness.
Stressing the second syllable; the stress belongs on BROO.

senses.definition: To work studiously, especially late into the night.
senses.example: He was burning the midnight oil to finish his paper.

core.definition: To work or study late into the night, usually because you have a lot to finish.

pronunciation.tip: 'The' reduces to 'thuh' before a consonant. Stress 'MID' in 'midnight' and 'OIL' at the end; 'oil' rhymes with 'boil'.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It shows dedication, though it can also imply overwork.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this idiom for students, professionals, and people with deadlines, such as 'I'll burn the midnight oil to finish this report.' It is informal and common in conversation. A natural reply is 'Good luck, I hope you get some sleep too.'

distinctions.note: Pull an all-nighter means staying awake through the whole night. Burn the midnight oil can mean working late for a few hours.
Work late is a neutral description. Burn the midnight oil adds the idea of extra effort and sacrifice.

collocations: burn the midnight oil before the deadline
burn the midnight oil on a project
burn the midnight oil for finals
have to burn the midnight oil

examples.everyday: I'm going to burn the midnight oil tonight to finish my tax forms.
examples.professional: We'll have to burn the midnight oil to get the model ready before Thursday's review.
examples.analytical: Medieval scribes often burned the midnight oil copying texts by lamplight, which is the literal origin of the phrase.

nuance.analogy: Like a lamp left glowing in a study long after the rest of the house has gone to sleep.
nuance.etymology: From the literal use of lamp oil for reading and writing late at night.
common_mistakes: Dropping 'the' and saying 'burn midnight oil'; the article is normally included.
Using it for literally burning something; it is always figurative.

burn-the-midnight-oil.etymology: Originally referring to the act of burning lamp oil in oil lamps for light at night.

conversation.text: I've been burning the midnight oil to finish this report by Monday.
She's burning the midnight oil studying for her final exams.
We burned the midnight oil before the launch, but it paid off.

senses.definition: Offering to write down a message for someone.

core.definition: A phone phrase offering to write down a message for a person who is unavailable.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on the first syllable of 'message', and the second syllable is a reduced vowel, so it sounds like 'MES-ij', not 'meh-SAJ'. 'Take a' links as 'tay-kuh'.

nuance.connotation: Helpful and polite; it shows professional courtesy when someone cannot answer.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this in offices and homes when the person being called is away, typically as a receptionist or colleague's assistant. A natural reply is 'Yes, please. Tell him Maria called about the invoice.' Include a callback number and a short reason. 'Can I take a message?' is more typical than 'Do you want to leave a message?' in business settings.

distinctions.vs: Would you like to leave a message?
distinctions.note: Both invite a message, but the first is an offer from the person answering, while the second is a question the caller answers.
A note is written text for yourself, while a message is information for another person.

examples.everyday: Sorry, Mike just stepped out. Can I take a message for him?
examples.professional: Hi, this is the front desk. Mr. Lee is in a meeting, so can I take a message and have him call you back?
examples.analytical: The offer to take a message transfers the responsibility for delivery to the answerer, which keeps the call productive even when the intended recipient is absent.

nuance.analogy: Like a sticky note on someone's desk: you capture the request so it does not get lost.
nuance.etymology: 'Message' comes from Latin missaticum, something sent, related to mittere, to send.
common_mistakes: Saying 'take messages' as a countable noun in the singular when a count noun is needed; use 'a message' or 'messages'.
Stressing the second syllable, which makes the word sound unnatural.

conversation.text: She's in a meeting right now. Can I take a message?
"Is Paul there?" "No, he just stepped out. Can I take a message?"
I'm sorry, he's on vacation this week. Can I take a message?

senses.definition: Asking a driver to stop and let you out.

core.definition: A request asking a driver to stop at your current location so you can get out of the car.

pronunciation.respelling: kan yoo drop mee awf HEER
pronunciation.tip: 'Drop' has a short vowel like 'top'. 'Off' links to 'me' and sounds like 'mee-AWF', while 'here' takes the stress. The r in 'here' is clear in American English.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and polite; it is a standard request in everyday driving.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this to friends, family, or rideshare drivers when they are near their destination. Rideshare apps let you adjust the pin, but saying it out loud is still common. A natural reply is 'Sure, right here?' or 'Yeah, no problem.' Use 'Can you drop me off at the corner?' for a more specific place.

distinctions.vs: Can you let me out here?
distinctions.note: 'Let me out' is more about opening the door; 'drop me off' is the usual phrase for taking someone somewhere.
Picking up means collecting someone at the start of a trip, while dropping off happens at the end.

collocations: drop me off at the station

examples.everyday: We're almost at the restaurant, so can you drop me off here? I'll walk the last block.
examples.professional: I'm meeting the client downtown, so can you drop me off here near the office entrance?
examples.analytical: The request depends on a shared understanding of location and convenience, which makes 'here' a deictic word that the driver must interpret in context.

nuance.analogy: Like a parcel delivered to the nearest doorstep instead of the far end of the street.
nuance.etymology: 'Drop' comes from Old English dropa, a drop of liquid; 'off' is an adverb meaning away from.
common_mistakes: Saying 'drop me here', which is understood but less natural; include 'off'.
Using 'drop out' instead of 'drop off', which means quitting a course or school.

conversation.text: This is close enough. Can you drop me off here?
Can you drop me off here? I'll walk the rest of the way.
"Can you drop me off here?" "Sure, let me pull over."

senses.definition: A richly decorative collar.

core.definition: A decorative necklace or collar, often made of jewels or precious metal, worn as an ornament.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, KAR. The second syllable is a reduced schwa, and the final syllable rhymes with 'bet'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive, with an old-fashioned, ornamental tone. It is used in poetry or historical fiction.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use carcanet in speech. You will mostly encounter it in older poetry, historical novels, or detailed descriptions of jewelry. In modern conversation, say 'necklace' or 'collar' instead. It is a good word to recognize in literature but not one to use often yourself.

distinctions.note: Necklace is the common everyday word, while carcanet is an old, literary term for a richly decorated necklace or collar.
A choker is a close-fitting necklace, usually worn snugly around the neck, while a carcanet is more often an elaborate, jeweled ornament.

examples.everyday: My grandmother wore a fancy old necklace, and she called it a carcanet, which sounded very old-fashioned.
examples.professional: The museum catalog describes the piece as a carcanet, so we should check the date before we label it as a necklace.
examples.analytical: The poet's image of a carcanet of stars turns the sky into an ornament that the speaker wears like a crown.

nuance.analogy: Like a fancy word for a necklace in an old painting: the meaning is the same, but the tone is more formal and historical.
nuance.etymology: From Old French carcan, a collar or necklace, of uncertain origin.
common_mistakes: Confusing carcanet with 'cardigan' or 'cardinal' because of the shared start.
Using carcanet in casual speech, where it will sound odd or overly poetic.

senses.definition: The action or motion of something that cascades.

core.definition: Happening in a chain reaction, where each event causes the next one, often spreading across a system or group.

pronunciation.tip: The stress stays on the -SKAY- syllable even when 'cascading' comes before a noun, as in 'cascading FAILures'. Don't put the stress on the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Usually negative when describing failures or problems, and neutral or positive when describing visual effects like cascading curtains.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'cascading' a lot in tech and business writing, as in 'cascading failure' or 'cascading updates'. In everyday talk it mostly describes visual things like water or hair. In casual conversation, 'domino effect' is a common alternative.
